newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ to unveil mandatory pension savings scheme.
newsitem.headline: NZ to unveil mandatory pension savings scheme.

text.p: New Zealand will unveil a compulsory pensions plan next week that is to be put to a referendum, and opponents on Friday predicted a big defeat in what is seen as an opinion poll on Treasurer Winston Peters.

A poll of 933 people by financial services group Colonial showed opposition to the scheme had risen to 63 percent from 59 percent in May. Those intending to vote for the plan, which is to be unveiled on Monday, had fallen from 30 percent to 24 percent.
A spokesman for opposition Labour Party leader Helen Clark said Labour expected a strong no vote, although the gap may yet close if the government's "self-help" message gains ground.

Under a coalition agreement sealed between Peters' New Zealand First and the conservative National Party last December, it was agreed that all government MPs would support the outcome of the referendum, which will be held in September.
But NZ First's support has plunged since then and many observers believe the pensions plan has become a focus of opposition to Peters, who has been dogged by minor scandals.
Free-market Act Party leader Richard Prebble, who also supports a compulsory pension scheme, said it would be unfortunate if anti-Peters feeling clouded the issue.
"I fear that may be right. But just because Peters is wildly unpopular, it is no reason (to vote against) a compulsory scheme," Prebble told Reuters.
Peters has argued that New Zealand needs to save more and that the current universal pension scheme is unsustainable.

However, Labour finance spokesman Michael Cullen has argued that there is no proof that such a scheme would lift savings, and could instead divert savings from farms and businesses, and from the repayment of mortgages, decreasing overall savings efficiency.
Peters' campaigned in last year's election promising a second tier scheme to supplement the existing universal pension.
But since then, he has outlined a scheme that would replace, rather than reinforce, the current scheme.

It would involve three cents, rising over time to eight cents, in the dollar of tax being placed in personal pension plans to be used to buy an annuity to deliver income equivalent to the current state pension.

That would suggest a required level of savings of about NZ$160,000 ($108,000) over a normal working life. But insiders have indicated that may be as low as NZ$116,000 in the final proposal -- making it more palatable to the public and also lowering the cost to the government of "topping up" the contributions of those unable to save enough.
The government estimates about 60 percent of men and fewer women will achieve the required level without a top-up.
It is clear the proposal will address some criticisms coming from women who say their lower earnings, shorter average working life and longer life expectancy could disadvantage them.
It is expected that the scheme will include a mechanism that would distribute savings by a couple equally to both.

Peters has said the compulsory payments required from individuals by the scheme will be offset by a series of proposed tax cuts starting with a three percent cut in 1997/98, already legislated for, followed by smaller cuts in subsequent years.
But critics say the tax cuts beyond 1998 are not assured.
Investment experts, meanwhile, have given a cautious thumbs-up to the broad outlines of the scheme revealed so far.
"We're broadly comfortable with the principles that (Peters) has indicated he is considering," Roger Gill, chief executive of the Investment Savings and Insurance Association, told Reuters.
The scheme would come into force in July 1998, but if the polls are correct and it is defeated, the more important issue will be the how to redesign the current universal scheme.
($ = 1.48 New Zealand Dollars)
